title: Two Children with a Cat and an Eel
title_original: Twee kinderen met een kat en een aal
description: A laughing boy holds a wriggling live eel in one hand while clutching a squirming, unhappy kitten by the scruff with the other. A little girl beside him giggles gleefully as the kitten tries to claw the slippery eel.
context: Judith Leyster was one of the few women admitted as a full master to the prestigious Haarlem Guild of Saint Luke. Long misattributed to Frans Hals, Leyster's work was rediscovered in the late 19th century. The painting illustrates the Dutch proverb 'He who holds an eel by the tail holds a cat,' meaning that deceitful people and slippery situations are impossible to control.
title_eng: Two Children with a Cat and an Eel

title: Young Man with a Cat
title_original: Junger Mann mit Katze

context: Judith Leyster (1609–1660), pioneering Dutch Golden Age master and member of the Haarlem Guild of St. Luke, captured spontaneous laughter and dramatic chiaroscuro in lively genre scenes of laughing children clutching pets.

context: Jordaens was, alongside Rubens and Van Dyck, the leading master of Antwerp Baroque painting, famous for full-blooded, boisterous genre scenes overflowing with robust Flemish vitality.

context: Snyders captured the kinetic ferocity of domestic animals with astonishing dynamism. In seventeenth-century homes, pantry fights were a real domestic hazard that broke expensive ceramic ware.
title_eng: Two Cats Fighting in a Pantry

title: The Virgin and Child with the Cat and Snake (Bartsch 63)
title_original: De Heilige Familie met de kat (B. 63)
collection: National Gallery of Art, Washington / Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam
description: Rembrandt's celebrated 1654 etching in which a domestic cat snuggles at Mary's hem while the Christ Child sleeps peacefully, contrasting home intimacy with Christ's foot crushing the serpent of original sin.
context: Rembrandt stripped away the pomp and clouds of Catholic counter-reformation art to reimagine the Holy Family as an ordinary, loving working-class Dutch family. The domestic cat rubbing Mary's dress elevates humble everyday intimacy into sacred grace.
title_eng: The Virgin and Child with the Cat and Snake (Bartsch 63)

title: The Barber Shop with Monkeys and Cats
title_original: Die Katzenakademie
artist: David Teniers the Younger / Flemish School
culture: Flemish (Brussels / Antwerp, Court of Archduke Leopold Wilhelm)
description: A witty Flemish satirical singerie and cat genre scene, depicting monkeys operating a bustling barbershop while cats are shaved and pampered in mock-human fashion.
context: David Teniers the Younger was the court painter and curator of the Archduke Leopold Wilhelm's gallery. His humorous animal academy paintings were prized by royal collectors across Europe for their technical brilliance and wit.
title_eng: The Barber Shop with Monkeys and Cats

title: Gerrit Dou, *Mousetrap in a Kitchen* & *Old Woman Reading* (Leiden, 1640s–1660s)

title_eng: Gerrit Dou, *Mousetrap in a Kitchen* & *Old Woman Reading* (Leiden, 1640s–1660s)

title: The Idle Servant: Cat Stealing a Plucked Duck
title_original: De luie dienstmeid (detail with thieving cat)
description: A kitchen maid dozes soundly with head in hand amidst scattered pots and pans, while the mistress of the house smiles at the viewer, pointing out the consequence of sloth: a sneaky calico cat that has climbed onto the table to make off with an expensive plucked roast duck.
context: Nicolaes Maes was Rembrandt's most accomplished genre pupil. The painting warns against the deadly sin of sloth (*acedia*), demonstrating that negligence by domestic servants inevitably invites predatory disorder into the well-ordered household.
title_eng: The Idle Servant: Cat Stealing a Plucked Duck

title: Old Woman Saying Grace: The Cat Tugging the Tablecloth
title_original: Het gebed zonder end (Old Woman Saying Grace)
description: An elderly pious woman with closed eyes and clasped hands prays devoutly over her simple meal of salmon, bread, and soup. At her side, an impatient domestic cat uses its claws to tug urgently at the corner of the heavy tapestry tablecloth, threatening to pull down the entire dinner.
context: Known in Dutch as *Het gebed zonder end* ('Prayer without end'), this masterpiece contrasts saintly spiritual detachment with raw animal hunger, illustrating the constant struggle between pious prayer and earthly worldly distractions.
title_eng: Old Woman Saying Grace: The Cat Tugging the Tablecloth

title: The Large Cat (De grote kat)
title_original: De grote kat (Hollstein 42)
medium: Engraving and etching on laid paper
collection: Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam (RP-P-OB-11.439) / Art Institute of Chicago
description: Rendered with microscopic engraved lines of dazzling tonal range, an enormous domestic cat reclines comfortably in a windowsill or stone embrasure with its paws tucked serenely beneath its chest. Through the dark opening in the wall behind it, an oblivious mouse peeks out from the masonry, completely unaware of the apex predator dozing inches away.
context: Visscher's *The Large Cat* is hailed as the supreme monumental feline portrait of the European Baroque. By dedicating a large, virtuoso copperplate print solely to a domestic cat—a scale normally reserved for royal princes and biblical heroes—Visscher celebrated the sovereign psychological presence of the cat in Dutch Golden Age domestic life.
title_eng: The Large Cat (De grote kat)

title: Diego Velázquez, *Las Hilanderas* ("The Spinners" or *The Fable of Arachne*, Museo del Prado, Madrid, c. 1657)
title_original: Diego Velázquez, *Las Hilanderas* ("The Spinners" or *The Fable of Arachne*, Museo del Prado, Madrid, c. 1657)

title_eng: Diego Velázquez, *Las Hilanderas* ("The Spinners" or *The Fable of Arachne*, Museo del Prado, Madrid, c. 1657)

title: Cat Crouching on the Ledge of an Artist's Atelier
title_original: De keukenmeid met kat
medium: Oil on panel with arched top
description: A breathtaking fijnschilder masterpiece by Gerrit Dou, featuring a tortoiseshell cat peering through an arched stone aperture directly toward the viewer, with painter's tools and an easel visible in the shadowed studio background.
context: Gerard Dou was Rembrandt's first pupil in Leiden and the founder of the *Fijnschilders* ('fine painters'), celebrated for microscopic brushwork that hid all surface traces of paint. Dou used arched niche compositions (*nisstukken*) to create astonishing illusions of physical reality extending into the viewer's space.
title_eng: Cat Crouching on the Ledge of an Artist's Atelier

title: An Old Woman Eating Porridge with a Cat
title_original: Oude vrouw die pap eet met een kat
description: An elderly grandmother in spectacles spoon-feeds herself barley porridge from an iron pot, while her patient tabby cat sits expectantly by her wooden clogs, eyes fixed on every movement of the spoon.
context: Metsu excelled at portraits of the elderly, exploring themes of patience, solitary contentment, and the comfort brought by humble domestic animals in old age.
title_eng: An Old Woman Eating Porridge with a Cat

title: Allegory of Night: The Concert of Cats and Owls
title_original: Allegory of Night: Concert of Animals
description: In a moonlit forest clearing, an assembly of nocturnal creatures gathers around an open musical score: a circle of cats sit upright meowing the notes, accompanied by screech owls, bats, and night moths fluttering in the silver moonlight.
context: Jan van Kessel was the grandson of Jan Brueghel the Elder, specializing in luminous, microscopic oil paintings on polished copper sheets. In Flemish folklore, the discordant nocturnal caterwauling of mating cats was humorously dubbed 'The Cat's Concert' (*Katzenkonzert*), symbolizing cacophony and unruly passion.
title_eng: Allegory of Night: The Concert of Cats and Owls

title: A Merry Party
description: Lively Dutch tavern interior where a boisterous family makes music, while an opportunistic cat watches the festive commotion from beneath the table.
context: Jan Steen (1626–1679), renowned Dutch Golden Age comedic painter, captured lively domestic disorder in tavern and home interiors. In his paintings, mischievous children teasing cats or cats sharing porridge dramatize Dutch proverbs on parental guidance and folly.
title_eng: A Merry Party

title: The Cat's Breakfast (Le Déjeuner du chat)
title_original: Het kattenontbijt
submovement: Dutch Golden Age High Genre Painting
description: In a peaceful Dutch kitchen flooded with soft diagonal window light, a modest young woman in a scarlet jacket and white cap feeds fresh fish morsels from an earthenware bowl to an eager cat that stands upright on its hind legs, resting its front paws politely on her apron.
context: Gabriel Metsu was a peer of Johannes Vermeer and Pieter de Hooch, celebrated for his silvery light effects and tranquil domestic refinement. Unlike Jan Steen's rowdy scenes, Metsu captures the quiet, mutual affection of everyday companionship between Dutch housewives and their household mousers.
title_eng: The Cat's Breakfast (Le Déjeuner du chat)

description: In an elaborate seventeenth-century surgeon-barber shop with apothecary jars and shaving basins, anthropomorphic cats perform haircuts, lather whiskers with soap, extract teeth, and bandage wounded limbs of customer cats seated in wooden chairs.
context: Barber shops in early modern Europe performed both cosmetic haircuts and bloody minor surgeries like bloodletting and tooth extraction. Van Kessel transformed human medical terrors into comedic animal satire.
title_eng: Cats with Still Life in a Pantry

collection: Musée des Beaux-Arts de Rouen, France
description: Six cats of various breeds gather around an open sheet of musical notation resting on a stool, singing loudly with open mouths while a conductor-cat with spectacles waves a baton.
context: Singeries and animal allegories satirized human vanity, ridiculing aristocratic salon singers whose screeching opera performances sounded to ordinary folk like caterwauling strays on a fence.
title_eng: The Cat Concert (Cats Singing from Musical Score)

title: The Cat Family (Children Teaching a Cat to Read)
title_original: Kinderen leren een poes lezen (De kattenfamilie)
description: In a noisy, chaotic Dutch tavern-kitchen, three laughing children gather around a wooden stool to teach an unimpressed tabby cat how to read: a mischievous boy forces round spectacle glasses onto the cat's nose while holding up a school primer, while his sister offers the protesting cat a spoon of porridge.
context: Jan Steen was the greatest comedic storyteller of the Dutch Golden Age, famous for the Dutch proverb 'a Jan Steen household' (*een huishouden van Jan Steen*), denoting affectionate domestic mayhem. The scene moralized against misdirected education: just as an owl or cat cannot learn to read no matter how many spectacles and candles you give it (*Wat baten kaars en bril als de uil niet zien en wil*), fools cannot be taught wisdom against their nature.
title_eng: The Cat Family (Children Teaching a Cat to Read)

context: Chardin reimagined traditional Dutch game still lifes with French eighteenth-century tonal delicacy and intimate kitchen observation.
title_eng: Still Life with Cat and Fish (Nature morte au chat et aux poissons)

title: The Ray (La Raie: The Bristling Cat among Oysters)
title_original: La Raie (The Ray-Fish)
description: Upon a stone kitchen slab, dominated by a gutted stingray hanging from a hook like a grotesque grinning phantom, an agitated calico cat steps gingerly across an open dish of oysters. The cat's back is stiffly arched, its claws tip-toeing delicately to avoid wet shells, its eyes wild and fearful as it sizes up the glistening seafood.
context: Submitted as Chardin's reception piece (*morceau de réception*) to the Académie Royale de Peinture et de Sculpture in 1728, *La Raie* astounded fellow painters, who initially thought it was the work of a celebrated Flemish master. The brilliant French critic Denis Diderot famously wrote that Chardin's paint was 'not mere pigment, but the very substance of things, the air and light itself.' The tense, trembling cat provides the sole living pulse within a monumental scene of biological mortality.
title_eng: The Ray (La Raie: The Bristling Cat among Oysters)

title: The Cat and the Two Sparrows (Fables de La Fontaine)
title_original: Le Chat et les deux moineaux (Livre XII, Fable 2)
medium: Brush and black ink, grey wash, heightened with white gouache on blue paper
collection: Musée Jean de La Fontaine, Château-Thierry / Metropolitan Museum
description: Illustrating Jean de La Fontaine's famous fable, a cunning pet cat that grew up alongside a tame sparrow intervenes in a fight between its friend and a wild visiting sparrow. After seizing and devouring the stranger, the cat turns to its childhood companion, remarking that sparrows taste far too delicious to spare.
context: Oudry's 275 illustrations for the *Fables de La Fontaine* are among the crowning achievements of 18th-century European graphic art, later engraved in four magnificent folio volumes. Oudry captured the cold, immutable predatory logic of the feline soul.
title_eng: The Cat and the Two Sparrows (Fables de La Fontaine)

title: La Toilette (Woman Fastening Her Garter with Cat)
title_original: La Toilette / Femme attachant sa jarretière
description: Inside an intimate boudoir decorated with a Chinese folding screen and porcelain fireplace mantel, an elegant young woman seated in an armchair lifts her petticoats to fasten a pink garter. At her feet, a fluffy white-and-grey kitten plays gleefully with a dropped spool of embroidery silk.
context: François Boucher was the favorite painter of Madame de Pompadour and Premier Peintre du Roi to Louis XV. In 18th-century Rococo erotic metaphor, the kitten playing with loose yarn beneath the lady's raised skirts was a playful, flirtatious symbol of sensual pleasure and feminine secrets.
title_eng: La Toilette (Woman Fastening Her Garter with Cat)

title: The Graham Children: The Menacing Cat Stalking the Caged Goldfinch
title_original: The Graham Children (detail with predatory cat)
description: In an ostensibly joyous portrait of the four children of Daniel Graham (apothecary to Chelsea Hospital), the young boy plays a bird-organ to make his caged goldfinch sing. In the upper right corner, perched menacingly atop the carved mahogany back of the boy's chair, the family cat glares with dilated, savage eyes, clawing the wood as it stalks the frantic, flapping caged bird.
context: Hogarth was the supreme satirist and moral commentator of Georgian London. The menacing cat stalking the caged bird is a poignant *memento mori*: unknown to the viewer, the youngest baby seated in the wicker go-cart (Thomas) had already died before the painting was finished. The cat embodies the sudden, inescapable predator of Death waiting to destroy innocent childhood happiness.
title_eng: The Graham Children: The Menacing Cat Stalking the Caged Goldfinch

medium: Pastel on paper mounted on canvas
description: A luminous portrait of a rosy-cheeked young girl in a blue bodice, cradling an exquisite grey tabby kitten close in her arms. The kitten rests its front paws against the girl's lace collar, its round blue-green eyes staring into the distance with pure innocence.
context: Perronneau was, alongside Maurice Quentin de La Tour, the undisputed French master of 18th-century pastel painting. Executed with velvety strokes of dry chalk pigment, this portrait captures the fragile bloom of childhood and the silky softness of a kitten's coat with supreme Rococo charm.

medium: Hanging scroll; ink and light color on paper

context: In Joseon Korea, *Myo* (cat) sounded like the word for old age, while *Jak* (sparrow) symbolized joyful good news. The painting was therefore an auspicious visual message wishing the recipient a long life filled with happy tidings.

title: The Mice are Burying the Cat (Funeral of the Cat of Kazan)
title_original: Мыши кота погребают (Похороны кота Казанского)
collection: State Historical Museum, Moscow / Hermitage Museum
description: In an elaborate satirical parade, dozens of joyful mice dressed in caftans and boots push, pull, and carry a giant bound cat upon a sled toward its grave. Mice play horns, beat drums, carry incense, and toast with mugs of vodka, while the cat feigns death with closed eyes, waiting for the procession to reach the graveyard before springing alive.
context: This legendary Russian folk print (*lubok*) carried potent political satire, widely interpreted by commoners and Old Believers as a mockery of the funeral of Tsar Peter the Great (who had forcibly shaved boyars' beards, introduced western dress, and instituted harsh taxes). The mice celebrating the tyrant's death served as a cautionary fable against premature celebration.

title: Le chat angora (The Angora Cat)
title_original: Le chat angora
description: Jean-Honoré Fragonard's celebrated oil painting 'Le chat angora' depicts a fluffy white Angora cat resting beside a decorative table. Revered for its exquisite rendering of silken feline fur and sparkling Rococo brushwork, it was formerly misattributed to Fragonard's sister-in-law Marguerite Gérard.
context: Jean-Honoré Fragonard (1732–1806), brilliant master of French Rococo painting, celebrated sensuous lightness and radiant color. His famous 'Le chat angora' (c. 1783–1785, Wallraf-Richartz-Museum, Cologne) showcases his virtuoso brushwork rendering the silken white coat of a prized Angora pet.

context: Marguerite Gérard was one of the most successful and financially independent female painters of late 18th-century France. The sister-in-law and pupil of Fragonard, Gérard lived and worked in his Louvre apartment, mastering the rendering of reflective silk satins and intimate domestic pet portraits.

context: Goya's *Red Boy* is one of the most haunting portraits in Western art. The three demonic, wide-eyed cats represent the dark predatory forces of the unconscious mind and the fragile boundary separating innocent childhood sheltered within aristocratic luxury from the brutal, lurking savagery of the real world.

collection: Museo del Prado, Madrid / Metropolitan Museum of Art
description: As the sleeping artist slumbers with his head resting upon his drawing desk, the nocturnal gloom erupts with flapping owls, bats, and at the foot of his stool, a giant, eerie feline with wide glowing eyes watching over the sleeper.
context: The central manifesto plate of Goya's legendary print series *Los Caprichos*. The watchful feline symbolizes nocturnal vigilance as well as the dark hallucinations and irrational superstitions that besiege human minds when rational intellect sleeps.

title: Mother Cat with Two Kittens
title_original: Katzenmutter mit zwei Kätzchen
description: An intimate watercolor drawing of a mother cat lovingly grooming the forehead of a small calico kitten, while a second kitten chases its mother's twitching tail in the background.
context: Gottfried Mind was an autistic Swiss savant whose extraordinary talent for drawing cats earned him the international nickname 'The Raphael of Cats' (*Der Katzen-Raffael*). Mind lived in poverty in Bern surrounded by beloved felines; when the city council ordered all cats killed during a rabies panic in 1809, Mind successfully hid and saved dozens of them, preserving their memory in hundreds of tender master drawings.

title: Sleeping Cat
title_original: Sleeping Cat
medium: Porcelain with overglaze color enamel and gold (Hizen ware)
description: Models of sleeping cats with collars and bells like this one were popular as decorative objects, and some of them also served as incense burners or hand warmers. This cat was just for display and has very carefully incised lines in the surface of the clay body, as well as thin strokes of orange and gold over the glaze to create the sense of soft fur.
context: Hizen ware porcelain produced in the Arita kilns of Kyushu during the Edo period, when decorative cat models were popular among Japanese collectors. Acquired by the Cleveland Museum of Art in 1964.

collection: American Folk Art Museum, New York (1984.1.1)
description: A young girl in a vibrant crimson off-the-shoulder dress with a coral bead necklace sits holding a small white kitten curled in her lap, while a spotted terrier sleeps under her stool. The stark geometric planes and glowing scarlet dress create an unforgettable American icon.
context: Ammi Phillips was one of the most prolific itinerant folk portraitists of 19th-century America, working across the Hudson Valley. Today, *Girl in Red Dress* is widely recognized as the supreme masterpiece of American folk art, celebrated for its bold chromatic contrast and pure linear abstraction.

title: Cats Suggested as The Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō
title_original: 東海道五十三対 其の侭地口 猫飼好五十三疋 (Sono mama jiguchi myōkai-kō gojūsan-hiki)
medium: Triptych of woodblock prints (nishiki-e); ink and color on paper
collection: Ōta Memorial Museum of Art, Tokyo / British Museum, London
description: Across three sweeping woodblock prints, Kuniyoshi depicts fifty-five individual cats engaged in hilarious puns (*jiguchi*) matching every post-town along the famous Tōkaidō highway: cats sleeping, stealing fish, catching mice, clawing tatami mats, and begging for treats.
context: Utagawa Kuniyoshi was the undisputed feline fanatic of art history, living in his Edo studio surrounded by dozens of cats who slept in his kimono sleeves. During the restrictive Tenpō Reforms when the shogunate banned portraits of kabuki actors and courtesans, Kuniyoshi brilliantly outsmarted the government censors by disguising actors and popular culture as playful cats.
title_eng: Cats Suggested as The Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō

title: Cats Suggested as The Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō (Full Triptych)
title_original: 流行猫の戯 (Ryūkō neko no tawamure)
medium: Woodblock print; ink and color on paper
collection: Ōta Memorial Museum of Art, Tokyo / British Museum
description: Anthropomorphic cats dressed in fashionable Edo kimonos, obis, and headscarves act out dramatic roles from popular Kabuki plays, brandishing miniature swords and striking exaggerated theatrical poses (*mie*).
context: When the Edo authorities prohibited prints of Kabuki stars to curb public extravagance, Kuniyoshi sidestepped the ban by drawing cats with facial expressions clearly identifying specific famous actors like Ichikawa Danjūrō, creating underground bestsellers.
title_eng: Cats Suggested as The Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō (Full Triptych)

title: Cat Print from Edo Women Series (Women 11)
title_original: 初鰹と猫 (Hatsugatsuo to neko)
description: A calico cat sinks its fangs greedily into a giant freshly-caught bonito fish (*katsuo*) lying on a straw kitchen mat, growling possessively with flattened ears.
context: Eating the first bonito of spring (*hatsugatsuo*) was an extravagant culinary obsession in Edo, with citizens famously joking they would pawn their wives just to taste it. Kuniyoshi humorously showed that Edo's cats shared the exact same gourmet greed.
title_eng: Cat Print from Edo Women Series (Women 11)

title: Minhwa Hojakdo: Magpie and Tiger/Leopard-Cat Under Pine Tree (호작도)
title_original: 민화 호작도 / 묘호도 (Minhwa Hojakdo / Myohodo)
medium: Mineral pigments on heavy mulberry paper (hanji)
description: A classic Korean Joseon folk painting (Minhwa) depicting a spotted feline and a chattering magpie in the boughs of an evergreen pine, representing joyful news and protective warding against evil spirits.
context: *Minhwa* were popular paintings created by itinerant artists for ordinary townspeople and farmers to paste on their front gates at New Year. While tigers were traditional, artists frequently substituted cats to add affectionate domestic comedy and ward off evil spirits (*byeoksa*).
title_eng: Minhwa Hojakdo: Magpie and Tiger/Leopard-Cat Under Pine Tree (호작도)

title: A Qajar Portrait of a Lady with a Cat
title_original: پرتره قاجاری بانویی با گربه
collection: Sotheby's Arts of the Islamic World / Private Collection
description: Luminous 19th-century Qajar court portrait of a royal Iranian noblewoman in richly embroidered brocade, gently cradling a white Persian cat with a fluffy tail. The work illustrates the high status of domestic and Angora cats in elite Persian households during the reign of the Qajar shahs.
context: During the Qajar period in Persia (1789–1925), cats held a privileged cultural place, prized both as elegant companions and symbols of luxury. Nasir al-Din Shah Qajar famously cherished his pet cat Babr-e Khan. This oil portrait combines Western linear perspective and modeling with traditional Persian decorative motifs and jewelry.

title: Vase
title_original: Vase
description: This vase vibrantly encapsulates the admiration for historical works of art and architecture that dominated the 1800s. It features stylistic qualities of ancient Egyptian, ancient Greek, and medieval Islamic art with its cat legs, amphora shape, and spiraling foliage ornamentation. The enameling technique itself, called champlevé, has roots in the ancient world. Champlevé enameling involves carving out sections of metal before filling those areas with colored enamel. The vase model was introduced at the International Exhibition of London in 1862, and its popularity resulted in several color and shape variations.
context: Cast and enameled by the Paris foundry of Ferdinand Barbedienne, this vase was introduced at the 1862 International Exhibition in London. It now resides in the collection of the Cleveland Museum of Art.
feline_symbolism: The cat-form legs evoke ancient Egyptian feline iconography, a historicist nod to the sacred status of cats in Pharaonic art. Here the cat serves as ornamental support rather than devotional subject.
title_eng: Vase

title: Olympia (The Arched-Back Black Cat at the Foot of the Bed)
title_original: Olympia (detail with black cat)
description: At the foot of the unmade bed where the nude courtesan Olympia reclines gazing unapologetically at the spectator, a black cat stands with its back arched in a sharp hump, tail standing straight up in alarm, and yellow eyes gleaming in startled defiance.
context: When exhibited at the Paris Salon of 1865, *Olympia* caused the greatest scandal in French art history. While Titian's *Venus of Urbino* placed a sleeping lapdog at the foot of the bed as an emblem of marital fidelity, Manet deliberately replaced the faithful dog with a bristling black alley cat—a slang symbol in 19th-century Paris for female sexuality, nocturnal vice (*chatte*), and bohemian rebellion. Baudelaire and Zola praised the cat as the defiant emblem of modern urban Paris.
title_eng: Olympia (The Arched-Back Black Cat at the Foot of the Bed)

title: Julie Manet with Cat (L'Enfant au chat)
title_original: Julie Manet au chat / L'Enfant au chat
description: Nine-year-old Julie Manet (daughter of Berthe Morisot and niece of Édouard Manet) sits in an armchair wearing a white collared dress, cradling a grey-and-white cat in her arms. The cat is closed in absolute ecstacy of pleasure, head tilted upward as it purrs against the child's shoulder.
context: Commissioned by Julie's parents Berthe Morisot and Eugène Manet, this painting represents the height of Renoir's *période aigre* (sour / Ingresque period), where he disciplined soft Impressionist light with crisp contours. Renoir had Julie pose for four sittings while holding her pet cat, producing one of the most sublime and psychologically tender portraits of child-animal communion in world art.
title_eng: Julie Manet with Cat (L'Enfant au chat)

location: Rare; known examples in private collections
description: A compact bronze of a cat arched in the characteristic washing posture, head turned downward toward its body, with a rough, expressive surface typical of Claudel's direct modeling. The form is tightly coiled, emphasizing the animal's flexibility and concentration.
context: Created around 1893, during the period when Claudel was distancing herself from Rodin and producing small 'sketches from nature.' Surviving casts are extremely scarce; the companion piece Dog Gnawing a Bone is held in the Museo Soumaya, Mexico City.
feline_symbolism: A pure study of feline self-absorption and physical grace, reflecting Claudel's shift toward intimate, non-allegorical observation of the everyday world after her break with Rodin.

title: Tournée du Chat Noir de Rodolphe Salis
title_original: Tournée du Chat Noir de Rodolphe Salis
submovement: Art Nouveau & Belle Époque Poster Art
medium: Color lithograph poster on wove paper (quattricolor)
collection: Zimmerli Art Museum at Rutgers University (Gift of Susan Schimmel Goldstein); Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam (RP-P-1969-78); Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam; Musée de Montmartre, Paris
description: The quintessential icon of Bohemian Montmartre: a hieratic, arching black cat with glowing yellow eyes, bristling whiskers, and a spiked medieval halo emblazoned with the cabaret's motto 'Montjoye Montmartre', perched atop a crimson pedestal against an ecru and cream ground. Printed as a large-format color lithograph (quattricolor) on wove paper, the poster's bold silhouette, flat planes of color, and sinuous Art Nouveau contour fuse Japanese ukiyo-e graphic economy with Byzantine halo iconography.
context: Created in 1896 to advertise the touring shadow-theatre cabaret of Rodolphe Salis's legendary establishment Le Chat Noir in Montmartre. Salis founded the cabaret in 1881; beginning in 1892 he organized a company of performers to tour during the summer months, and Steinlen's poster served as a 'coming attractions' announcement posted outside host venues. Steinlen, one of the artists whose career was launched at the Chat Noir, here permanently canonized the black cat as the universal emblem of avant-garde artistic independence, nocturnal bohemianism, and Parisian counterculture. Impressions are held by the Zimmerli Art Museum at Rutgers University (Gift of Susan Schimmel Goldstein, photo by Jack Abraham), the Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam (RP-P-1969-78), the Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam, and the Musée de Montmartre, Paris.
title_eng: Tournée du Chat Noir de Rodolphe Salis
location: Zimmerli Art Museum at Rutgers University (Gift of Susan Schimmel Goldstein); Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam (RP-P-1969-78); Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam; Musée de Montmartre, Paris
feline_symbolism: The black cat functions as the heraldic emblem of Le Chat Noir cabaret and, by extension, of Montmartre's bohemian avant-garde: a creature of the night associated with artistic independence, irony, and countercultural freedom. The spiked (radiant) halo and the motto 'Montjoye Montmartre' (a medieval war-cry) sacralize the animal, elevating a stray alley cat to an icon of artistic sanctity and nocturnal sovereignty.

feline_symbolism: Sensual indolence, bourgeois leisure, and the playful affinity between female intimacy and feline agility.

title_original: Mädchen mit Katze
medium: Tempera and oil on canvas mounted on cardboard
description: A monumental, earthy peasant girl with dark hair holds an orange-tabby cat close in her arms. Both the child and the feline are rendered with raw, heavy sculptural forms, muted earth pigments, and an uncompromising, primitive directness of gaze.
context: Paula Modersohn-Becker was the first female artist in world art history to paint nude self-portraits and one of the pivotal pioneers of Early Expressionism before her tragic death from an embolism at age 31. Working in the rural artists' colony of Worpswede, she stripped away salon sentimentality to capture the archaic, timeless bond between humans and animals.

context: René Lalique made the choker in France around 1906–1908; Calouste Gulbenkian acquired it from the artist in 1920. It now belongs to the Gulbenkian Collection.
feline_symbolism: Cats appear as engraved naturalistic motifs alternating with foliage, part of Lalique's late Art Nouveau vocabulary of animal and plant forms.

context: Matisse was the triumphant leader of the *Fauves* ('Wild Beasts'), liberating color from descriptive reality to serve pure emotional expression. title: Kuroki Neko: Black Cat on an Oak Branch
title_original: 黒き猫 (Kuroki Neko)
medium: Hanging scroll; ink and mineral pigments on silk (*morotai* technique)
collection: Eisei Bunko Museum, Tokyo (Important Cultural Property of Japan)
description: Perched securely upon the lichen-encrusted branch of a red oak tree surrounded by drying autumn leaves, an elegant black cat gazes directly outward with luminous green eyes. Its glossy fur is painted without harsh outlines, blending into the atmosphere through delicate misty gradations.
context: Painted in just five days for the 4th Bunten Exhibition shortly before Shunsō's tragic death at age 36, *Kuroki Neko* is officially designated an Important Cultural Property of Japan. Shunsō pioneered the revolutionary 'morotai' (vague / outline-less) painting style, harmonizing traditional Japanese mineral pigment aesthetics with Western impressionist light and atmospheric depth.
title_eng: Kuroki Neko: Black Cat on an Oak Branch

title: Manor House in Jankówka (Meeting of Cats)
title_eng: Manor House in Jankówka (Meeting of Cats)
title_original: Dworek w Jankówce (pierwotnie: Spotkanie kotów)
description: Two family cats—Maciek, a grey tabby, and Czarcik, a slender black cat—meet nose-to-nose on a garden path edged with dahlias, roses and sunflowers. Beyond them the white south façade of the eighteenth-century wooden manor at Jankówka rises under a bright sky, its veranda draped in climbing plants.
context: Mehoffer bought the larch-wood manor at Jankówka in autumn 1907 and designed its terraced garden; he owned it until 1917. Originally titled Spotkanie kotów ('Meeting of Cats'), the canvas is a principal record of the estate, demolished in 1946, and is held by the National Museum in Kielce.
feline_symbolism: The two cats turn a garden view into a private family scene; their cautious approach gives the painting an intimate, storybook mood, as if a small fairy tale were unfolding among the flowers.

title: Cat Behind a Tree (Katze hinter einem Baum)
title_original: Kinderbild (Katze hinter einem Baum)
description: In an abstract Bavarian mountain meadow, a luminous golden cat peers curiously from behind the purple trunk of a tree, its curved spine echoing the rhythmic rolling green hills in the distance.
context: Marc wrote passionately: 'Is there a more mysterious idea for an artist than to imagine how nature is reflected in the eyes of an animal? How does a horse see the world, or an eagle, or a cat?' In this painting, the cat is not an object within landscape, but the conscious soul of the landscape itself.

description: A cat curls tightly upon a radiant yellow cushion surrounded by dark violet shadows, painted with expressive, rhythmic color planes.

title: Cats, Red and White (Katzen, rot und weiß)
title_original: Katzen, rot und weiß
description: Curled in a rhythmic, harmonious circle upon a vibrant patchwork of primary colored pillows, a pure white cat slumbers in sublime spiritual tranquility. The geometric planes of yellow, cobalt blue, and vermilion radiate outward from the white feline body like sacred energy waves.
context: Franz Marc was a co-founder of the avant-garde movement *Der Blaue Reiter* (The Blue Rider) with Wassily Kandinsky. Marc sought to see the world through the uncorrupted eyes of animals, which he regarded as pure spiritual beings untainted by modern human alienation and violence. In Marc's personal color symbolism, white stood for pure light, blue for spiritual masculinity, and yellow for gentle, sensual joy.
title_eng: Cats, Red and White (Katzen, rot und weiß)

context: Influenced by Robert Delaunay's Orphism and Italian Futurism, Marc synthesized animal form into universal cosmic rhythms shortly before his tragic death at the Battle of Verdun in 1916.

feline_symbolism: The kitten is the absurd centre of a mock-serious medical and social drama, reflecting Witkacy's affection for cats and his satirical humour.

title: Cat and Flowers
title_eng: Cat and Flowers
title_original: 猫と花 (Neko to Hana)
description: A pastel drawing on paper depicting a domestic cat amid a profusion of flowers. Tanaka Yasushi renders the feline with soft, atmospheric pastel strokes, the animal's form emerging from a field of floral color. The work exemplifies the artist's Paris-period synthesis of Japanese sensibility and French modernist drawing, characterized by delicate tonal transitions and an intimate, decorative still-life sensibility.
context: Tanaka Yasushi (1886–1941) left Japan after graduating from Saitama Prefectural Urawa High School in 1904, traveling alone to Seattle to study painting. He later moved to Paris in 1920 with his wife, exhibiting at the Salon d'Automne and other periodic salons, and never returned to Japan; he died in Paris in 1941. This work, dated 1920–1940, is held by the Museum of Modern Art, Saitama (MOMAS).
feline_symbolism: The cat appears as a companion animal within a floral still life, embodying domestic intimacy and the quiet poetry of everyday life rather than mythic or heraldic significance. In Tanaka's expatriate oeuvre, such subjects reflect the artist's turn toward intimate, decorative observation of the Parisian interior.

title: Sitting Cat
title_eng: Sitting Cat
title_original: Chat Assis
dimensions: 6 in. L x 3.75 in. W x 8.125 in. H (15.2 cm x 9.5 cm x 20.6 cm)
description: A seated cat in colorless mold-pressed glass sits upright with its tail wrapped forward between its legs, ears alert and head gently turned. Subtle modeling across the shoulders and flanks suggests musculature, while textured passages evoke fur against smooth chest and legs. Light moves through the clear glass, giving the small statuette a calm, poised presence.
context: René Lalique designed the model on 23 February 1932, after establishing his Wingen-sur-Moder glassworks in 1921. This example is signed LALIQUE France on the base and was offered at Artemis Fine Arts from a private Wellington, Colorado collection; a comparable example is held by the Corning Museum of Glass (2011.3.413).
feline_symbolism: In early twentieth-century decorative arts, the cat carried associations of elegance, independence, and mystery; Lalique reduces the animal to essential curves, treating it as a refined sculptural form rather than a caricature.

title: Chat
title_eng: Chat
title_original: Chat
medium: Pressed molded glass, satin-finished and polished
description: A lidded box of pressed molded glass with a cat's head in relief on the lid. Satin-finished areas contrast with polished sections, bringing out the expressive eyes, long radiant whiskers, and delicate facial contours. Signed "R. Lalique" on the underside of the base.

Two seals complete the sheet.

title: Drawing for Plate 8: Folk Art of Rural Pennsylvania (Seated Cat)
title_original: Cat and Kittens (American Folk Painting)
description: On a vivid emerald-green ground, an enormous, wide-eyed domestic calico cat sits upright with triangular ears and stiff white whiskers, accompanied by two tiny kitten clones playing with a ball of red yarn. The composition is rendered with bold graphic flatness, intense geometric symmetry, and mesmerizing decorative clarity.
context: Untrained itinerant American painters ('limners') traveled throughout rural New England painting portraits and domestic animals for middle-class farmers and merchants. Unburdened by academic rules of anatomical shading and atmospheric perspective, naive folk painters created striking, direct graphic icons that were later passionately embraced by modernists as authentic American folk vision.
title_eng: Drawing for Plate 8: Folk Art of Rural Pennsylvania (Seated Cat)

description: A long-haired kitten with black-and-white fur is shown from behind, turning to watch a butterfly fluttering before it. context: Xu Beihong painted this ink-and-wash work in 1944. It belongs to his animal painting and uses traditional Chinese brushwork to capture a fleeting, tender encounter between a kitten and a butterfly.

title: A Cat Caught a Bird (Кіт схопив пташку)
title_original: Кіт схопив пташку (Звір гуляє)
medium: Gouache on paper (Commemorative State Art Edition)
collection: National Museum of Ukrainian Folk Decorative Art, Kyiv, Ukraine
description: In Ukrainian folklore, the cat is both a domestic hearth guardian and a mystical creature mediating between domestic and supernatural worlds. Prymachenko's visionary cat radiates magical power, transforming ancient Slavic animism into vibrant modern folk symbolism.
context: Maria Prymachenko's fantastical creatures emerged from deep roots in Ukrainian Polissya folklore and pagan decorative traditions. Despite personal tragedies including World War II and the Chornobyl disaster, she continually painted vivid, protective animal spirits. In 'A Cat Caught a Bird', her feline beast combines fierce predatory power with ornate, peaceful flower-patterns, demonstrating her belief in nature's transcendent spiritual equilibrium.
